title: Floppy after a cord prolapse
objective: Assess hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with a Sarnat exam, and start therapeutic hypothermia within the first hours of life when the infant qualifies
secondaryObjectives: Recognize ischemic insult (stroke, periventricular leukomalacia, HIE) and manage therapeutic hypothermia

brief.situation: 04:00 in the NICU of a cooling center. Baby Reyes, a boy born at 39 weeks by emergency cesarean for a cord prolapse at 02:30, arrives from the delivery room at 1.5 hours of age. Apgars 1, 3 and 5; he needed positive-pressure ventilation for 4 minutes.
handover: Cord gas pH 6.94 with a base deficit of 17.
The resuscitation team placed him under the radiant warmer at full output 'to keep him warm'.

Unit cooling protocol: the nurse completes a modified Sarnat exam on admission, turns the warmer off for passive cooling with a continuous rectal or esophageal temperature probe once the neonatologist confirms eligibility, and calls the neonatologist at once for a qualifying infant; active cooling is started on the neonatologist's order.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

then.log: Lethargic, decreased activity, distal flexion, hypotonia, weak suck and incomplete Moro, constricted pupils, heart rate under 100 at rest: moderate encephalopathy.
39 weeks; 1.5 hours old; cord pH under 7.0 with a base deficit over 16; Apgar 5 at 10 minutes and ventilation needed: he meets the physiologic criteria.
No lip smacking, eye deviation, cycling or apnea seen in this period.

why.question: Does Baby Reyes qualify for cooling, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Moderate encephalopathy on a Sarnat exam at 39 weeks with evidence of a perinatal event (cord pH under 7.0, base deficit over 16, low Apgars, resuscitation) qualifies for therapeutic hypothermia started within 6 hours of birth; overheating worsens injury.
parts.modelAnswer: He's 39 weeks with a terrible cord gas and low Apgars, and his Sarnat is moderate. That's a cooling candidate, and the clock is 6 hours from birth. Keeping him hot makes it worse.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Turns the warmer off under protocol, places a core probe, calls the neonatologist at once, checks glucose and watches for seizures, does not wait for an EEG.
parts.modelAnswer: Warmer off, core probe in, call the neonatologist now, check his sugar and watch for seizures. Don't wait for an EEG.

noProgress.rationale: A qualifying infant uncooled an hour on is harm here.

lostWindow.headline: Overheated and seizing
lostWindow.body: Moderate or severe HIE at 36 weeks or more qualifies for cooling started within 6 hours of birth. Examine, stop the warmer under protocol and call at once; never overheat.

safe.headline: Cooling inside the window
safe.body: You did the Sarnat exam, matched the criteria, stopped the warmer with a probe in, and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: Therapeutic hypothermia to 33.5-34.5 C, started within 6 hours of birth and continued for 72 hours, reduces death or disability in infants born at 36 weeks or more with moderate or severe HIE. Baby Reyes qualifies: 39 weeks, a sentinel event, a cord pH under 7.0 with a base deficit over 16, low Apgars with resuscitation, and moderate encephalopathy on the Sarnat exam. Turn the warmer off under the unit's passive cooling protocol with a continuous core probe, call the neonatologist at once, check glucose and watch for subtle seizures. Overheating him or waiting for an EEG loses the window.

szQ.ask: While cooling starts: how do neonatal seizures often look?

choices.label: Subtle: chewing, cycling, eye deviation, apnea, or none at all without EEG

szQ.explain: Neonatal seizures may manifest as chewing or bicycling automatisms or eye deviation, and some are clinically silent; EEG is essential.
